questions.knowledge_point: Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle
questions.problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{5}{9}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{5}{9} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{4}{9} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $x=\frac{2}{3}.$

The point $P$ lies on the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of $P$ is $\frac{3}{7},$ use the Pythagorean Identity to find $sin⁡\theta .$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931905/assets/cb569d4b7b76699259d2167b8c930e636e3fb794b14ef25a4d909c224235d7c3.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{3}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
cos⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{3}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{40}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So our final answer is $sin⁡\theta =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}$

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{\sqrt{15}}{5}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$

$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{15}}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{15}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{10}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}.$

Knowing that $csc⁡\theta =\frac{1}{sin⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}csc⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5})}=\frac{5}{\sqrt{10}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}csc⁡\theta  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{10}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{10}}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{10}}{10} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{24}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}.$

Knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5})}=\frac{5}{2\sqrt{6}}.
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡\theta  & =\frac{5}{2\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{5}{2\sqrt{6}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{6}}{2\cdot 6} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{6}}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $\dfrac{5}{9}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $A?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
x^2+y^2=1 .
$$

Substituting $y=\dfrac{5}{9}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\eqalign{
		x^2+y^2&=1\[5pt]
	        x^2+\left(\dfrac{5}{9}\right)^2&=1\[5pt]
		x^2+\left(\dfrac{25}{81}\right)&=1\[5pt]
		x^2&= 1-\dfrac{25}{81}\[5pt]
		x^2&= \dfrac{56}{81}\[5pt]
		x&= \sqrt{\dfrac{56}{81}}\[5pt]
	        x&= \pm \dfrac{2\sqrt{14}}{9}.
}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive. So, we select the positive answer. 

Therefore, our final answer is $x=\dfrac{2\sqrt{14}}{9}.$

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\dfrac{2}{3},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.
$$

We're given that $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{4}{9}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{5}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $\sin\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. 

So our final answer is $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 5}{3}.$

$$

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{2\sqrt 6}{7}$ gives
